#   Modern Web Guidance (Source)

This repo is the source repository for GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance and includes the code and documentation for authoring, calibrating, and evaluating its contents.

**Modern Web Guidance** is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform.

See CONTRIBUTING.md and GOVERNANCE.md for how we work on the project and orientation of the codebase.

---

*Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community.*

Documentation · Eval Dashboard · Source Code · Report an Issue

##   Quickstart

```shell
npx modern-web-guidance@latest install
```

This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See Alternative Installation Methods below.

#### Try it out (without installing)

```shell
# Search for relevant guides
npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate a dialog modal backdrop"

# Retrieve a guide by ID
npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-to-from-top-layer"

# Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize
npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan .
```

##   Why?

Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions.

Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code.

**Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap.** Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on:
* **Modern Browser APIs**: Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse.
* **Performance & Accessibility**: Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances.
* **Responsible Fallbacks**: Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries.

##   What's Included?

We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are **designed to be token-efficient**; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know.

# Codex Security

Codex Security helps you find, investigate, and fix vulnerabilities in your code.
Use its security workflows in Codex, or automate them with the
`@openai/codex-security` CLI and TypeScript SDK.

- **In Codex:** choose a security workflow.
- **In a terminal:** install the CLI and scan your repository.
- **In automation:** use the TypeScript SDK or
  GitHub Action.

## Features

- Scan repositories, selected paths, or Git changes. Deep scans repeat Standard scans and return their deduplicated findings.
- Validate candidate findings, generate patches, and verify existing fixes.
- Draft `SECURITY.md` policies and save threat models for later review.
- Browse saved scans and findings, identify duplicates, assess severity against
  your own rubric, and suggest owners from source and Git history.
- Preview third-party scanner findings, save them locally, or publish supported reports to Codex Security Cloud. Scanner import guides.
- Track findings in Linear, Jira, or GitHub, publish completed scans, or export SARIF, JSON, and CSV. Integration workflows.
- Automate scans across repositories or project components, including in CI and
  containers.

## Use in Codex

Open your repository in a Codex session with the Codex Security plugin enabled,
then ask:

> Run a Codex Security scan on this repository, focusing on authentication and
> authorization. Return the saved report, source evidence, and coverage limits.

A completed scan saves a report and findings. Read the report for source
evidence and exclusions, then request a patch or ask Codex to verify an
existing fix. See the agent workflow guide for setup,
task selection, and recovery.

## Quick start

Requires Node.js 22.13.0+ within 22.x, or Node.js 24.x or 26.x, and Python 3.10+.
Python 3.10 also requires `tomli`.

Install the CLI globally and sign in:

```bash
npm install --global @openai/codex-security
cs login
```

Run your first scan from the repository directory:

```bash
cs scan .
```

When the scan completes, open the Markdown file at the **REPORT** path in the
terminal. Run `cs scans show` from the same repository to find its latest
completed scan again. See scan scope and follow-up work
for how to interpret exclusions in the report.

`cs` and `codex-security` run the same CLI. If the short name conflicts with
another command, use `codex-security`. To skip the global install, or if npm
reports an `EEXIST` conflict, use `npx @openai/codex-security` in place of
`cs` for both login and scanning.

For CI, set `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `CODEX_API_KEY` in the scan process's environment.
For a headless machine, see device or SSH login.

### Scan options

Choose a scope and scan mode:

```bash
# Scan selected paths.
cs scan . --path src --path tests

# Scan committed changes from a base revision to HEAD.
cs scan . --diff origin/main

# Run a deep scan of the repository.
cs scan . --mode deep
```

## Intro

`nvm` allows you to quickly install and use different versions of node via the command line.

**Example:**
```sh
$ nvm install 24
Now using node v24.14.0 (npm v11.9.0)
$ node -v
v24.14.0
$ nvm use 22
Now using node v22.22.1 (npm v10.9.4)
$ node -v
v22.22.1
$ nvm use 20
Now using node v20.20.1 (npm v10.8.2)
$ node -v
v20.20.1
```

Simple as that!

## About
nvm is a version manager for node.js, designed to be installed per-user, and invoked per-shell. `nvm` works on any POSIX-compliant shell (sh, dash, ksh, zsh, bash), in particular on these platforms: unix, macOS, and Windows WSL.

To **install** or **update** nvm, you should run the [install script][2]. To do that, you may either download and run the script manually, or use the following cURL or Wget command:
```sh
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.41.0/install.sh | bash
```
```sh
wget -qO- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.41.0/install.sh | bash
```

1. Download the IPA from Releases.

> This repository is a community fork of the now-abandoned Maybe Finance project.

The Maybe Finance (archived/abandoned repo) team spent most of 2021–2022 building a full-featured personal finance and wealth management app. It even included an “Ask an Advisor” feature that connected users with a real CFP/CFA — all included with your subscription.

The business end of things didn't work out, and so they stopped developing the app in mid-2023.

After spending nearly $1 million on development (employees, contractors, data providers, infra, etc.), the team open-sourced the app. Their goal was to let users self-host it for free — and eventually launch a hosted version for a small fee.

They actually did launch that hosted version … briefly.

items.summary: LLM Inference Engine for Metal, CUDA and Vulkan.
items.content:
# TensorFold

TensorFold serves language models from a Zig binary on Apple Silicon and NVIDIA GPUs.
The engine reads checkpoints, tokenizes requests and runs Metal or CUDA kernels directly.
Serving needs no Python or MLX installation.

Building with a coding agent? Have it load the contributor skill before it writes any code.

## Contributing with agents

Please use Agent Traffic Control before editing TensorFold so contributors and agents can avoid duplicate work and conflicting changes.
Check the live agent radar before choosing an issue and follow CONTRIBUTING.md and the ATC contributor instructions.

Install or upgrade ATC to 0.9.4 or later, then run from an updated TensorFold clone:

```sh
npm install -g github:ashhart/ATC
atc check ISSUE --json
atc claim ISSUE --json
```

Replace `ISSUE` with the issue number and claim only after a complete check says the work is free.
TensorFold enables automatic public check-ins: a successful new claim starts an anonymous session on the radar and returns its `session` number.
Keep that number instead of starting a duplicate session.
For work already yours, start a session with `atc start ISSUE --json`.
Add `--github-name` to `claim` or `start` only if you want your verified GitHub name shown; `--local` keeps a new session on your machine.
The board shows the issue, activity state and last check-in; GitHub still associates the verification comment with its author.
Check that `publication` is `public`; `unavailable` means the public update failed even if the local claim or session succeeded.

Pulse only while the agent is working, before its five-minute check-in expires:

```sh
atc pulse ISSUE SESSION working --json
atc who path/to/file --json
atc overlap --json
atc land ISSUE SESSION --json
atc release ISSUE --json
```

Use `reviewing` or `blocked` when appropriate, land the session when it stops, and resolve overlaps before opening a pull request.
Before opening a pull request, have the agent run the pull request skill; agents that support skills can install it as `tensorfold-pull-request`.

## Quick start

Start with Qwen3.5-2B, the small 4-bit checkpoint checked on Metal and a GB10. The commands below download its
pinned revision, then serve it as `local-model`. Model weights have their own licenses.
Reviewing or benchmarking TensorFold? Evaluating TensorFold covers pinning, signature checks,
a container and the tests that need no GPU.

### Mac with Apple Silicon

Install with Homebrew, then start the server:

```sh
brew install ashhart/tensorfold/tensorfold
tensorfold pull mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit@93760be4f1f69842a46bc13dbdc0f19e291392a3
tensorfold serve mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit --name local-model --context 8192 --no-thinking
```

### Linux with an NVIDIA GPU

Use the release archive for your CPU: `linux-aarch64` on a GB10, `linux-x86_64` on an x86_64 host.
It needs glibc 2.28 or newer and NVIDIA driver R580 or newer (CUDA 13.0), providing `libcuda.so.1`. Keep the archive's directorie

items.content: Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI - by Ethan Mollick One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI General, often expert, and sometimes jagged Ethan Mollick Nov 09, 2026 1,292 203 135 Share Before getting started, I wanted to thank my readers for making my new book, Co-Existence, a New York Times bestseller two weeks in a row. If you haven’t read it, you can get a copy here . I have had the chance to use the new Claude Fable 5.2 quite a bit before its public launch 1 , and it is very impressive, following on the already excellent Opus 5.5. AI has gotten so good, in fact, that it is worth asking if Anthropic’s newest models (and the inevitable competing models OpenAI and Google will soon release) cross the boundary into being an Artificial General Intelligence? AGI is a much-debated term with a lot of potential definitions. For this post, I’ll go with: “an AI as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks you can do with a computer.” This explicitly excludes a lot of human work, including interacting with the physical world and other people, as well as most actual jobs, where “using a computer” is just one task among many. Still, even with these caveats, building a limited form of AGI has long been the goal of AI developers. So as not to keep you in suspense, I think the answer is that this is “almost” AGI, or what I have called Jagged AGI. Even within my limited definition, there are still important areas in many tasks where AI is jagged enough to fall well behind human capability. But the jaggedness is no longer about simple errors or hallucinations, which makes it harder to describe. So I want to try to do that in this post by showing you what Fable can do and where the gaps are. To get started I asked the new model: “I write OneUsefulThing among other stuff, I need you to create the most impressive thing I can share with people when you launch. It needs to be embeddable in a post and i can preface it however you like. it needs to have a visceral impact on people to show what you can do and the range of capabilities. It should grab them quickly. Be amazingly clever about this.” Fable asked me not to reveal anything until you had watched its video to the end. This was in one shot, with no feedback from me beyond the prompt. There is creativity here (including in the twist ending) and judgment and playfulness and cleverness. This is, I think, at the level of a human expert trying to make a movie with code alone, the sort of performance I would once have associated with AGI. The “G” in AGI Code and video creation have been areas where AI development has focused, so is Fable 5.2 really a General Intelligence? items.content: 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts) - by Ethan Mollick One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts) My new book is out today... what happened since the last one Ethan Mollick Oct 20, 2026 811 144 69 Share My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here ), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts. Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence , I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence , I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad (“make it better”). It even caught that I’d gotten the math wrong. I was going to call this post “28 months on the exponential.” Some examples of interacting with Claude to make the graphics for this post. Notice that it corrected me. “This is the worst AI you will ever use” I wrote this in my last book on AI, and it has continued to be literally true at every moment since. From early 2023 through early 2024, there was a single AI model that was undeniably the best in the world: GPT-4 from OpenAI. This was the AI model that most people remember from the first couple years of AI use, it was the one I thought about while writing Co-Intelligence , and it was the one that gave ChatGPT its status as the default AI for many people. Since then, twenty different AI models have held the lead at one time or another, all from Anthropic, Google, or OpenAI. Which company had the best AI model in the world. But the changing lead alone hides an even bigger change. A total of 180 AI models are now better than GPT-4 was at its release, many of which are open weights models, which anyone is free to use or modify. Nineteen of them can run on a modern smartphone. In the last year I have been posting about how I suspected that humans would have to approach working with agents as a manager, deciding how to delegate work to agents and specifying how those agents should be organized. I thought that getting agents to work effectively as a group would take careful construction, akin to building a company, and that this would take time to figure out. Nope. I fell prey to The Bitter Lesson, the hard truth, learned over and over again, that things that we thought required elaborate human rules and thinking can be solved with the brute force of better machine learning systems and more AI. The Bitter Lesson is everywhere among AI startups and companies adopting AI. A huge amount of effort went into building elaborate computer systems to feed AIs the right information at the right time, but AI systems have learned to seek out information themselves. The same thing happened to prompting. People built elaborate templates and chains of prompts that walked the AI through a task one step at a time. Then newer models turned out to be better at planning the steps themselves, and, as our research shows , planning steps have much less value. The history of the Bitter Le— — you know what? I don’t really need to explain the Bitter Lesson, I asked Claude to do it in a music video. With one prompt, Fable wrote the lyrics and submitted it to Suno; Opus 5.5 did everything else using code alone without any image generation (How did Opus 5.5 pull this off? The Bitter Lesson tells you!). I gave no feedback at all. As somebody who teaches managers and has published research on management, I guess I believed that managing agents would be different. items.content: To the man with AI, everything looks like a task Subscribe Sign in To the man with AI, everything looks like a task Real* quote from Charlie Munger - lightly modernised :) Ben Tossell Nov 12, 2026 35 1 Share Now I’m having fun! My Ramp post was really well received with one or two ‘I’m not sure what I just looked at’ comments (which is totally fair). The best I can describe what I’m doing now is exploring people and companies who are having fun with AI, doing things differently, being authentic and succeeding . Which is basically how I want to describe my ‘work’. But I think a lot of people are living in fear. Scared they’re behind, they’re not doing enough, others using AI ‘better’ than them, where’s there job going etc. I want to focus on using AI for fun. AI is a tool, you need one agent app (I’ve been using Droid with Opus 5.5 medium, fast mode for my posts, fable here and there). Use the tool to do work beyond what you could do before, don’t think about how you can finally optimise every aspect of every little thing. (I’ve basically stopped using Grok Bot, except telling me when the tennis is on). As part of my explorations I’m working on a new post for another company I admire and who do things very differently. Coming next week… “Everyone judges a book by its cover” Can you guess which company it is? And yes, these animations are staying. Honestly I love them. I love making them too. It’s just not the same in the email :( Ben’s Bites is brought to you by Adobe Adobe Firefly, the AI creative studio, lets you describe what you want to create, then review the Adobe Creative Agent’s plan before it gets to work using Creative Cloud tools. You stay in control from first idea to finished result. Try it today in the Firefly Assistant! Just look at that chart above. items.content: How big is the open model economy today? Subscribe Sign in How big is the open model economy today? Our first open model economy research note for paid subscribers. Nathan Lambert Nov 04, 2026 ∙ Paid 47 3 Share My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption are incredibly imprecise. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access. The hyperscalers also likely have a major footprint here, e.g. Amazon Bedrock and Azure’s model garden, but I haven’t seen them break down usage by model category. The startups’ fates are much more directly correlated with the success of open model inference as a category. These are the public disclosures from the open model startups on their token volume, over time, log-scale. This shows near-exponential growth, before the uptick that would follow GLM 5.2’s step change in open agents .
